cards.title: Introdution
body: World War I (WW I), also known as the Great War, lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918.WW I was fought between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. The main members of the Allied Powers were France, Russia, and Britain. The United States also fought on the side of the Allies after 1917.The main members of the Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria.

cards.title: The causes of WWI: long-term and immediate
body: **Long-term causes (remember "MAN").** **M**ilitarism – the great powers built huge armies and navies; **A**lliances – the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, 1882) against the Triple Entente (France, Britain, Russia, 1907); **N**ationalism – each state put its national interest first and competed for colonies and trade.
**The Balkan spark.** Serbia, backed by Russia, wanted a large Slav state; Austria-Hungary annexed **Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908**, which angered Serbs.

**Immediate cause.** On **28 June 1914** Gavrilo Princip, a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb linked to the Black Hand, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife in **Sarajevo**. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war; the alliances pulled the other powers in within weeks.
**Exam tip:** Always separate the long-term causes (MAN) from the immediate cause (Sarajevo).

steps.text: Dates: 28 July 1914 – 11 November 1918 (the "Great War").

cards.answer: From 1914 to 1918 the Allies (France, Russia, Britain, later the USA) fought the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Bulgaria).

cards.title: Causes of the War
body: There was no single event that led to World War I. The war happened because of several different events that took place in the years building up to 1914.

The new international expansionist policy of Germany: In 1890 the new emperor of Germany, Wilhelm II, began an international policy that sought to turn his country into a world power. Germany was seen as a threat by the other powers and destabilized the international situation.

Mutual Defense Alliances: Countries throughout Europe made mutual defense agreements. These treaties meant that if one country was attacked, allied countries were bound to defend them. The Triple Alliance-1882 linking Germany with Austria-Hungary and Italy. The Triple Entente, which was made up of Britain, France, and Russia, concluded by 1907.Thus, there were two rival groups in Europe.

Imperialism: Before World War I, Africa and parts of Asia were points of contention among the European countries because of their raw materials. The increasing competition and desire for greater empires led to an increase in the confrontation that helped push the world into World War I.

Militarism: As the world entered the 20th century, an arms race had begun. By 1914, Germany had the greatest increase in military buildup. Great Britain and Germany both greatly increased their navies in this time period. This increase in militarism helped push the countries involved into war.

Nationalism: Much of the origin of the war was based on the desire of the Slavic peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina to no longer be part of Austria Hungary but instead be part of Serbia. In this way, nationalism led to the War.

cards.title: Model answer: long-term causes of the First World War
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the long-term causes of the First World War.

steps.text: Alliances: the Triple Alliance (1882: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) vs the Triple Entente (by 1907: Britain, France, Russia) – an attack on one drew in its allies.
Imperialism: competition for colonies and raw materials in Africa and Asia.
Militarism: an arms race – Germany's huge build-up and the naval race with Britain.
Nationalism: Slavs in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to join Serbia rather than stay in Austria-Hungary; Germany's world-power policy under Wilhelm II added tension.

cards.answer: Rival alliances, imperial competition, militarism and nationalism (remember MAIN) made a general war likely.

cards.title: The immediate cause
body: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand: In June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot while he was visiting Sarajevo in Bosnia. He was killed by a Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Principe , who thought that Serbia should control Bosnia instead of Austria. Because its leader had been shot, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. As a result Russia got involved as it had an alliance with Serbia. Germany then declared war on Russia because Germany had an alliance with Austria-Hungary.

Britain declared war on Germany because of its invasion of neutral Belgium - Britain had agreements to protect both Belgium and France. Some of the major battles during the war included the First Battle of the Marne, Battle of the Somme, Battle of Dannenberg, Battle of Gallipoli, and the Battle of Verdun.

cards.title: Model answer: from assassination to world war
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain how the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand led to a general war.

steps.text: June 1914: Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, was shot in Sarajevo by the Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Princip.
Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia; Russia, Serbia's ally, got involved.
Germany, Austria-Hungary's ally, declared war on Russia.
Germany invaded neutral Belgium, so Britain, pledged to protect Belgium and France, declared war on Germany.

cards.answer: The alliance system turned the Sarajevo assassination into a chain of declarations of war: Austria–Serbia, Russia, Germany, then Britain after Belgium was invaded.

lessons.title: Course of the First World War

cards.title: Course of the First World War
body: The conflict developed on several fronts in Europe, Africa, and Asia. The two main scenarios were the Western front, where the Germans confronted Britain, France and, after 1917, the Americans. The second front was the Eastern front in which the Russians fought against Germans and Austro-Hungarians.

cards.title: How the war was fought on the two fronts
body: **Western Front.** Germany planned to reach Paris quickly through **Belgium** (war on Belgium 4 August 1914) and got within 40 km of Paris, but was stopped at the **Marne** – France even rushed troops to the front in 2,000 Paris taxis.

**Stalemate.** Both sides dug trenches from the English Channel to Switzerland, protected by barbed wire, mines and machine guns, with "no-man's land" between them. Generals sent masses of men across after artillery barrages, and millions died; at **Verdun (1916)** about 700,000 died for a few kilometres.

**Eastern Front.** More mobile: Russia was beaten in eastern Germany, but Russia and Serbia drove Austria-Hungary out of Serbia; German help then defeated Russia (2.5 million casualties) and knocked Serbia out.
**New weapons.** Aircraft (first scouting, then attacking), submarines, machine guns, tanks and poison gas.
**Memory trick:** "West = trenches and stalemate; East = movement and huge losses."

cards.title: The western front
body: The war zone that included Belgium and northern France was called the Western Front. Germany had a plan to invade France through Belgium that’s why it invaded Belgium in august 4 which led to the entry of Great Britain to the war.

Once the Germans failed to reach Paris, the war quickly turned into a stalemate. Both the French and German forces dug hundreds of kilometers of trenches that stretched from the English Channel to the frontiers of Switzerland. These trenches were protected by barbed wire, land mines, and machine guns. They were separated from each other by a strip of territory known as no-man’s land.

The new method of fighting (Trench Warfare or War of Attrition) was new to the 1st world war generals. The no man’s land was unbreakable though they send thousands of soldiers. In 1916, for example, seven hundred thousand soldiers died over a few kilometers of land at Verdun, France.

cards.problem: (Exam question) Why did the Western Front become a stalemate?

steps.text: Plan failed: Germany invaded France through Belgium but failed to reach Paris.
Trenches: both sides dug hundreds of kilometres of trenches from the English Channel to Switzerland, protected by barbed wire, mines and machine guns.
No-man's land: attacks across it cost thousands of lives for little ground.
Example: about 700,000 died at Verdun (1916) over a few kilometres – a war of attrition.

cards.answer: When the German advance stopped short of Paris, both sides dug in; defensive weapons made attacks across no-man's land suicidal, producing a war of attrition.

cards.title: II.The Eastern Front
body: On the Eastern Front, Russia and Serbia fought against Austria-Hungary, Germany, and Turkey. In contrast to the Western Front, the war on the Eastern Front was marked by mobility. The cost in lives, however, was equally enormous.

At the beginning of the First World War, the Russian army moved into eastern Germany. But, it was decisively defeated. On the other hand, Russia and Serbia defeated Austria-Hungary and threw it out of Serbia. To make matters worse, the Italians betrayed their German and Austrian allies and attacked Austria in May 1915.

After it was defeated by Russia and Serbia, Austria-Hungary got help from its ally, Germany. Then the combined forces of Germany and Austria-Hungary defeated the Russian army. Russia suffered a very heavy casualties of 2.5 million killed, captured or wounded. It was almost knocked out of the war. Encouraged by their success, Germany and Austria-Hungary attacked and eliminated Serbia from the war.

cards.answer: A mobile front where Russia was defeated by Germany, and Austria-Hungary – first beaten by Russia and Serbia – recovered with German help to knock out Serbia.

cards.title: Widening (Spread) of the War
body: After the stalemate in western front different empires and countries were drawn to the war. Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria joined the central powers in 1915 .On May 1915 Italy turned to the allies. By 1917, the war that started in Europe became a world war. Britain encouraged Ottoman provinces in the Middle East to revolt against the Ottoman Empire. In 1918, British forces destroyed the Ottoman Empire in the Middle East. The Allied powers also took advantage of Germany’s preoccupation in Europe and its lack of naval power to seize German colonies in Africa and elsewhere. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and China also joined the war on the side of the Allies.

cards.title: Why the USA entered the war (1917)
body: **Blockades.** Britain blockaded Germany; Germany answered with unrestricted submarine warfare. **Lusitania (May 1915).** About 1,100 civilians, over 100 of them Americans, were killed; Germany paused its attacks. **1917.** Germany restarted unrestricted submarine warfare; the USA declared war in **April 1917**, and by 1918 over a million American soldiers were in Europe, tipping the balance.
**Memory trick:** "Subs sank ships, so the States stepped in."

cards.problem: (Short answer) How did the European war become a world war?

steps.text: New members: the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria joined the Central Powers (1915); Italy joined the Allies (May 1915).
Middle East: Britain encouraged Ottoman provinces to revolt and destroyed Ottoman power there in 1918.
Colonies: the Allies seized German colonies in Africa and elsewhere.
Worldwide: Japan, Australia, New Zealand and China joined the Allies; by 1917 it was a world war.

cards.answer: New members, fighting in the Middle East and the colonies, and the entry of Japan, Australia, New Zealand and China turned it into a world war by 1917.

cards.title: The entry of USA
body: At first the United States tried to remain neutral. As World War I continued, however, it became more and more difficult to remain neutral. The immediate cause of the United States entry into the war was a naval conflict between Germany and Great Britain.

In May 1915, a British ship named Lusitania was sunk by a German submarine. As a result, about 1100 civilians, including over 100 Americans, were killed. This greatly angered the United States. After strong opposition from the US, Germany stopped its unrestricted submarine attacks in 1915.

However Germany restarted sinking hundreds of allied ships killing thousands of civilians and On May 1917 USA officially entered in to the war sending one million troops. This greatly shifted the balance of power to the favor of the allies.

cards.title: 7.3 The Russian Revolution
body: The Russian revolution was a clash between the aristocratic monarchy of Tsar Nicholas 2nd and the people of Russia. The people specifically demanded peace and bread (the withdrawal of Russia from WW1 and economic reforms. Several causes led to the revolution of 1917 such as:
Industrially and technologically weak army.
Economic disasters caused by the war.
Tsar Nicholas 2 frequently usage of the army to suppress the people.

cards.title: Completing this point: causes and course of the Russian Revolution of 1917
body: **Causes.** (1) Russia was not ready for war – poor leaders and weak industry; two million soldiers died in 1914–1916 and four to six million were wounded or captured. (2) The war wrecked the economy. (3) Tsar Nicholas II ruled by force.

**February/March revolution.** Bread rationing in Petrograd led to protests; on **8 March 1917** (International Women's Day) about 10,000 women marched shouting "Peace and Bread". Soldiers refused to fire and joined them. The Duma set up a provisional government, and the tsar abdicated on 15 March.

**Bolsheviks take over.** Kerensky's provisional government stayed in the war. Lenin returned in April promising "Peace, Land, Bread" and "All Power to the Soviets", and on the night of **6 November 1917** the Bolsheviks seized the Winter Palace.
**Memory trick:** "War + Want + Whip = Revolution."

cards.title: Past exam (Model exam 2022)
cards.q: One of the following was **not** the cause of Russian Revolution of 1917:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “The Russian revolution was a clash between the aristocratic monarchy of Tsar Nicholas 2nd and the people of Russia.”

**Step 2:** **Analysis:** 
- **Causes (A, B, C, E):** Economic hardship, food shortages (bread riots), heavy military losses in WWI, and the absolute, suppressive rule of the Czar were all primary causes of the revolution.
- **The Assassination (D):** Czar Nicholas II and his family were assassinated in July 1918, which was a **consequence** or an event during the civil war *after* the revolution had already started in 1917.

**Step 3:** So the answer is D) Assassination of Czar Nicholas II.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the causes of the Russian Revolution of 1917.

steps.text: Political: the aristocratic monarchy of Tsar Nicholas II, who often used the army to suppress the people.
Military: an industrially and technologically weak army losing the war.
Economic: disasters caused by the war, including rising bread prices.
Popular demand: "peace and bread" – withdrawal from the war and reform.

cards.answer: Tsarist oppression, military defeat and war-time economic collapse made the people demand peace and bread, leading to revolution in 1917.

cards.title: The Beginning of the Revolution
body: In February 1917, the Russian government started bread rationing in the then capital city of Russia Petrograd (formerly known as St. Petersburg) after the price of bread had risen sharply. However this erupted an uprising in the capital city by thousands of women on 10th March, 1917. As usually Tsar Nicholas 2nd ordered the troops to fire upon the mob but the soldiers refused and sided with the uprising. This eventually ignited the 1917 revolution.

cards.title: From bread riots to the tsar's abdication (March 1917)
body: **Step 1 – hunger.** Bread prices rose sharply and rationing began in Petrograd in February 1917.
**Step 2 – the women march.** On **8 March** (International Women's Day) about 10,000 women marched shouting "Peace and Bread" and "Down with the Czar"; other workers joined and factories closed.
**Step 3 – the army changes sides.** Soldiers ordered to fire refused and joined the protesters.
**Step 4 – new government.** On **12 March** the Duma set up a **provisional government**; Nicholas II abdicated on **15 March 1917**.
**Step 5 – dual power.** Kerensky's provisional government stayed in the war, while the **soviets** (workers' and soldiers' councils, strongest in Petrograd) opposed it – which gave Lenin his chance.
**Memory trick:** "Bread → Women → Soldiers → Duma → Abdication."

cards.title: The effects of the revolution
body: On 12 March 1917, the Russian legislative body known as Duma established a provisional government headed by Alexander Kerensky.
The provisional government decided to continue Russia’s involvement in the First World War.
The above decision led to protest from different protest groups especially the Soviets (The Soviets were local councils composed of representatives of Russian workers and soldiers).

The rise of the Bolsheviks; ‘Bolsheviks’ meaning majority in Russian, was a small faction of the Russian Marxist party known as the Social Democratic party. It was formed by a Russian Marxist named Vladimir I. Lenin in 1903.

Lenin and his comrades arrived at Petrograd, they began to unite the Soviets. They promised the people the following three things: “Peace, Land, Bread;” “Worker Control of Production;” “All Power to the Soviets.”
In November 6, 1917, the Bolshevik forces seized the Winter Palace (the seat of the provisional government). The provisional government quickly collapsed with little bloodshed.

cards.title: The result of the October 1917 revolution war
body: The congress appointed Lenin as head of the new government (communist).
In March 1918, Lenin signed the peace treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany and ended Russia’s involvement in the war.
Besides, the Bolshevik government nationalized all land and distributed them to the peasants.
The rise of civil war because of the opposition groups like the royalists, anti-Lenin socialists, and liberals.
The liberals in general known as the white force helped by the allied forces fought against the red army of the Bolsheviks .The red army decisively won in 1920.

cards.title: The Russian Civil War (1918–1921)
body: **Two sides.** The **Reds** (Communists) against the **Whites** – liberals, anti-Lenin socialists and royalists, backed by the Allies (at one point over 100,000 Allied troops were in Russia).
**Outcome.** The Red Army defeated most Whites by 1920 and controlled all Russia in 1921.
**The royal family.** Held in the Urals, the tsar, his wife and five children were killed by the local Soviet on the night of **16 July 1918**.

lessons.title: The end of the first World War

cards.title: The end of the first World War
body: Finally after the German offensive in the spring of 1918, the Allied counterattack managed to force a decisive retreat of the German army. The defeat of its Germany’s allies and the revolution in Germany that dethroned Wilhelm II (German Emperor), brought about the signing of the armistice on November 11, 1918. The Great War was over.

cards.title: How WWI ended, step by step
body: **1917 – mixed year.** Allied attacks on the Western Front failed and Russia left the war after the November revolution, but US entry raised Allied morale.
**March 1918 – Germany's last gamble.** Free from the Eastern Front, Germany attacked in the west and by April was within about 80 km of Paris.
**The turn.** French, Moroccan and American troops with hundreds of tanks stopped the advance; with over a million Americans in France the Allies counter-attacked and pushed steadily towards Germany.

**Collapse at home.** Defeats and hardship led to a German army mutiny in November 1918; workers' and soldiers' councils took over in the north, and **Emperor William II** left the country on **9 November**.
**Armistice.** The new government signed it on **11 November 1918**; Germany's allies (Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Bulgaria) had already given up.
**Cost.** Over 10 million soldiers and at least 1 million civilians died, and 20 million were wounded.
**Memory trick:** "11th hour, 11th day, 11th month, 1918."

cards.title: Consequences of the war
body: Economic consequences: World War I cost the participating countries a lot of money. Germany and Great Britain spent about 60% of the money their economy produced. Countries had to raise taxes and borrow money from their citizens. They also printed money in order to buy weapons and other things they needed for war. This led to inflation after the war.

Political Consequences: World War I brought an end to four monarchies: Czar Nicholas II of Russia, Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany, Emperor Charles of Austria and the sultan of the Ottoman Empire had to step down.

New countries were created out of old empires: Austria- Hungary was carved up into a number of independent states. Russia and Germany gave land to Poland. Countries in the Middle East were put under the control of Great Britain and France. What was left of Ottoman Empire became Turkey.

Social Consequences: World war changed society completely. Birth rates declined because millions of young men died (eight million died, millions wounded, maimed (to lose limbs), widows and orphans). Civilians lost their land and fled to other countries.
The role of women also changed. They played a major part in replacing men in factories and offices. Many countries gave women more rights after the war had ended, including the right to vote.
The upper classes lost their leading role in society. Young middle and lower class men and women demanded a say in forming their country after the war.

cards.title: Treaty of Versailles: On June 28, 1919
body: World War I officially ended with the signing of the Treaty of Versailles. The Treaty of Versailles was an attempt to prevent the world from going into another war. It is organized in several chapters each having different clauses.

cards.title: The Paris Peace Conference and the main terms of Versailles
body: **The Big Four.** Wilson (USA), Clemenceau (France), Lloyd George (Britain) and Orlando (Italy). Wilson wanted a League of Nations and borders based on nationality; France wanted huge reparations and a buffer state on the Rhine; Britain wanted reparations. The result was a compromise.
**Five treaties.** With Germany, Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and Turkey; Versailles (with Germany) was the most important.

**Four key terms.** (1) **War guilt** – Germany was responsible and must pay **reparations**; (2) army cut to **100,000** men, navy reduced, no air force; (3) **Alsace-Lorraine** returned to France; (4) the **Rhineland** demilitarized.
**Why it mattered.** Germans saw it as a harsh, humiliating dictated peace – one root of WWII.
**Memory trick:** "Guilt, Guns, Ground, Gold" – blame, disarmament, lost land, reparations.

cards.problem: (Exam question) What were the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles (1919)?

steps.text: Date and aim: signed on 28 June 1919 to end WWI and prevent another war.
Territory: France regained Alsace-Lorraine, Poland took eastern lands, Danzig became a free city, and Germany lost all its colonies.
Military: the German army was limited to 100,000 troops, with no tanks, aircraft or heavy artillery, a much smaller navy and a demilitarised Rhineland.

cards.title: Territorial clauses
body: *France regained Alsace and Lorraine from Germany.
*Eupen and Malmedy passed into the hands of Belgium from Germany.
*Eastern territories were annexed by Poland which caused East Prussia to become territorially isolated.
*Danzig and Memel, former Baltic German cities were declared free cities.
*Denmark annexed northern Schleswig-Holstein.
*Germany lost all of its colonies and the victors annexed them.
Military clauses:
*Drastic limitation of the German navy. Dramatic reduction of the Army (only 100,000 troops, prohibition of having tanks, aircraft and heavy artillery).
*Demilitarization of the Rhineland region.

cards.title: The wider territorial changes after WWI
body: **Empires broken up.** Austria-Hungary disappeared; Germany and Russia lost land in Eastern Europe. **New states.** Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Austria and Hungary. **Ottoman lands.** Despite promises to the Arabs, France took **Syria and Lebanon** and Britain took **Iraq and Palestine** as League of Nations **mandates**.
**Memory trick:** "Four empires fell, eight states rose."

cards.title: War Reparations
body: The treaty declared Germany and its allies responsible for all 'loss and damage' suffered by the Allies and as a consequence they were forced to pay war reparations to the victors.

cards.title: Reparations: the numbers and the consequences
body: **The bill.** In April 1921 the Allied Reparations Commission set the total at **132 billion gold marks** (about 33 billion US dollars), paid in yearly instalments. Germany made its first payment in 1921.

**The crisis.** In 1922 Germany said it could not pay. In 1923 France occupied the **Ruhr**, Germany's industrial heart, to take payment in coal and goods. German workers went on strike and the government paid them by printing money.
**Hyperinflation.** In 1914 one dollar bought 4.2 marks; by November 1923 one dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks, and savings were wiped out.
**The fixes.** The **Dawes Plan (1924)** lowered yearly payments according to Germany's ability to pay and gave a $200 million US loan, bringing a short prosperity (1924–29).
**The long-term effect.** Reparations caused resentment that Hitler used against the "Versailles dictate".
**Memory trick:** "132 billion → Ruhr → Runaway prices → Rescue (Dawes)."

cards.title: Other Treaties
body: *The Treaty of Neuilly, signed with Bulgaria. The small Balkan country suffered several territorial losses, in the benefit of Romania, Greece and a brand-new country: Yugoslavia.

*The Treaty of Sevres (1920) signed with Turkey .The Treaty of Sevres was extremely hard and led to the Turkish national rebellion, which was led by Kemal Ataturk. This also led to the war against Greece, which occupied large areas of Anatolia.
*other important social and ideological changes The U.S., which had won the war but had not experienced the conflict on its territory, became a first world power.
The triumph of the Soviet Revolution (Russian Revolution) and the social crisis that followed the war encouraged workers in many countries to protest, creating a pre-revolutionary climate.

The extreme nationalism experienced during the war, coupled with fear of a Communist revolution, encouraged the middle-class populations of some countries to move to the extreme right. This created a hotbed of fascist movements.

Creation of the League of Nations: The League of Nations was an international diplomatic group developed after World War I as a way to solve disputes between countries before they erupted into open warfare. A precursor to the United Nations, the League achieved some victories but had a mixed record of success.

tips.text: World War I (WW I), also known as the Great War, lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918.WW I was fought between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. The main members of the Allied Powers were France, Russia, and Britain. The United States also fought on the side of the Allies after 1917.The main members of the Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria.
There was no single event that led to World War I. The war happened because of several different events that took place in the years building up to 1914.

Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand: In June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot while he was visiting Sarajevo in Bosnia. He was killed by a Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Principe , who thought that Serbia should control Bosnia instead of Austria. Because its leader had been shot, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. As a result Russia got involved as it had an alliance with Serbia. Germany then declared war on Russia because Germany had an alliance with Austria-Hungary.

The conflict developed on several fronts in Europe, Africa, and Asia. The two main scenarios were the Western front, where the Germans confronted Britain, France and, after 1917, the Americans. The second front was the Eastern front in which the Russians fought against Germans and Austro-Hungarians.

cards.back: World War I (WW I), also known as the Great War, lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918.WW I was fought between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. The main members of the Allied Powers were France, Russia, and Britain. The United States also fought on the side of the Allies after 1917.The main members of the Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria.
There was no single event that led to World War I. The war happened because of several different events that took place in the years building up to 1914.

Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand: In June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot while he was visiting Sarajevo in Bosnia. He was killed by a Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Principe , who thought that Serbia should control Bosnia instead of Austria. Because its leader had been shot, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. As a result Russia got involved as it had an alliance with Serbia. Germany then declared war on Russia because Germany had an alliance with Austria-Hungary.

cards.front: Course of the First World War
cards.back: The conflict developed on several fronts in Europe, Africa, and Asia. The two main scenarios were the Western front, where the Germans confronted Britain, France and, after 1917, the Americans. The second front was the Eastern front in which the Russians fought against Germans and Austro-Hungarians.

The war zone that included Belgium and northern France was called the Western Front. Germany had a plan to invade France through Belgium that’s why it invaded Belgium in august 4 which led to the entry of Great Britain to the war.

On the Eastern Front, Russia and Serbia fought against Austria-Hungary, Germany, and Turkey. In contrast to the Western Front, the war on the Eastern Front was marked by mobility. The cost in lives, however, was equally enormous.

After the stalemate in western front different empires and countries were drawn to the war. Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria joined the central powers in 1915 .On May 1915 Italy turned to the allies. By 1917, the war that started in Europe became a world war. Britain encouraged Ottoman provinces in the Middle East to revolt against the Ottoman Empire. In 1918, British forces destroyed the Ottoman Empire in the Middle East. The Allied powers also took advantage of Germany’s preoccupation in Europe and its lack of naval power to seize German colonies in Africa and elsewhere. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and China also joined the war on the side of the Allies.

At first the United States tried to remain neutral. As World War I continued, however, it became more and more difficult to remain neutral. The immediate cause of the United States entry into the war was a naval conflict between Germany and Great Britain.
